chapter_sections.label: Definition:
chapter_sections.text:
A NUMBER SYSTEM is the collection of numbers and the rules for operations on
them. In this chapter we study natural numbers, whole numbers, integers, rational
numbers, irrational numbers and real numbers — together called the real number
system.

chapter_sections.label: Key Points:
points: Number line: A line on which all real numbers can be represented.
Number sets and symbols:
N = Natural numbers: 1, 2, 3, ...
W = Whole numbers: 0, 1, 2, 3, ...
Z = Integers: ..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ... (Z from German "zahlen" = "to count")
Q = Rational numbers: all p/q where p, q are integers, q ≠ 0
(Q from "quotient"; Rational from "ratio")
R = Real numbers: all rational + irrational numbers
Relationship: N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R

items: - Topic 1.3: Real Numbers and their Decimal Expansions
- Topic 1.5: Laws of Exponents for Real Numbers
EXAMPLES: (Chapter-level overview — see topic-level for full examples)
All 20 textbook examples are covered topic-wise below.
Examples 5–10 under Topic 1.3, Examples 11–19 under Topic 1.4,

items.question: Define a rational number. Give two examples.
items.answer:
A number 'r' is called a RATIONAL NUMBER if it can be written in the form p/q,
where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Symbol: Q (from "quotient").
Examples: 3/4 (p=3,q=4) and -5/2 (p=-5,q=2) are rational numbers.
Note: Every integer m = m/1, so all natural numbers, whole numbers, and integers
are also rational numbers.

items.question: Define an irrational number. Give two examples.
items.answer:
A number 's' is called an IRRATIONAL NUMBER if it CANNOT be written as p/q,
where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0.
Examples:
- sqrt(2) = 1.41421356... (non-terminating non-recurring) — irrational.
- pi = 3.14159265... (non-terminating non-recurring) — irrational.
Discovery: Pythagoreans in Greece first discovered irrationals around 400 BC.

items.question: What are the two types of decimal expansions of a rational number?
items.answer:
1. TERMINATING: Division ends (remainder = 0) after finite steps.
Example: 7/8 = 0.875.
2. NON-TERMINATING RECURRING: Division never ends; a block of digits repeats.
Example: 1/3 = 0.3bar.
Converse: Any number with terminating or non-terminating recurring decimal
expansion is RATIONAL.

items.question: State four laws of exponents for a > 0 and rational p, q.
Find five rational numbers between 3/5 and 4/5.
items.answer:
Step 1: Need 5 numbers → use denominator = (5+1)×5 = 30.
Step 2: 3/5 = 18/30 and 4/5 = 24/30.
Step 3: Five rationals between 18/30 and 24/30:
19/30, 20/30, 21/30, 22/30, 23/30.
Step 4: Simplified: 19/30, 2/3, 7/10, 11/15, 23/30.
Answer: 19/30, 2/3, 7/10, 11/15, 23/30.
(Infinitely many rational numbers lie between any two rational numbers.)

items.question: Express 0.2353535... as p/q form.
Rationalise 1/(7+3sqrt(2)) and verify.
items.answer:
Step 1: Conjugate of (7+3sqrt(2)) = (7-3sqrt(2)).
Step 2: Multiply num. and denom. by conjugate:
= (7-3sqrt(2)) / [(7+3sqrt(2))(7-3sqrt(2))].
Step 3: Denominator = 7^2-(3sqrt(2))^2 = 49-9×2 = 49-18 = 31.
Step 4: Result = (7-3sqrt(2))/31.
Verification: (7-3sqrt(2))/31 × (7+3sqrt(2)) = (49-18)/31 = 31/31 = 1. ✓
Answer: 1/(7+3sqrt(2)) = (7-3sqrt(2))/31.

items.question: Simplify using identities (state each identity):
items.answer:
(i) Identity: (a+sqrt(b))(a-sqrt(b))=a^2-b. Here a=5, b=5.
= 25-5 = 20.

(ii) Identity: (sqrt(a)+sqrt(b))^2=a+2sqrt(ab)+b. Here a=3, b=7.
= 3+2sqrt(21)+7 = 10+2sqrt(21).

(iii) Identity: (sqrt(a)+sqrt(b))(sqrt(a)-sqrt(b))=a-b. Here a=11, b=7.
= 11-7 = 4.

(iv) 8sqrt(15)÷2sqrt(3) = (8/2)×sqrt(15/3) = 4×sqrt(5) = 4sqrt(5).

Answer: (i) 20  (ii) 10+2sqrt(21)  (iii) 4  (iv) 4sqrt(5).

PART A:

(i) Long division of 1/7:
0.142857...
7  | 1.0000000
7
30, 28 → 2; 20, 14 → 6; 60, 56 → 4; 40, 35 → 5; 50, 49 → 1 (repeats)
Remainders: 3,2,6,4,5,1 → cycle repeats.
1/7 = 0.142857bar — NON-TERMINATING RECURRING.
Why block < 7: Non-zero remainders when dividing by 7 can only be 1 to 6
(max 6 distinct values). Once a remainder repeats, decimal repeats.
So block length ≤ 6 < divisor 7. ✓

(ii) 1.27bar to p/q:
Let x = 1.272727... Two digits (27) repeat → ×100:
100x = 127.2727... = 126 + 1.2727... = 126 + x.
99x = 126 → x = 126/99 = 14/11.
Verification: 14÷11 = 1.272727... = 1.27bar ✓

PART B:

(iii) Locating sqrt(2) on number line:
Step 1: Draw unit square OABC (each side = 1 unit).
Step 2: By Pythagoras: OB = sqrt(1^2+1^2) = sqrt(2).
Step 3: Place O at origin on number line.
Step 4: Compass radius = OB. Centre O. Arc meets number line at P.
Result: P represents sqrt(2). ✓

(iv) 0.10110111011110...:
Pattern: 1,0; 11,0; 111,0; 1111,0 — number of 1s keeps increasing.
No fixed repeating block ever forms.
Non-terminating and NON-RECURRING → IRRATIONAL.

sections.label: Definition:
sections.text:
A number 'r' is called a RATIONAL NUMBER if it can be written in the form p/q,
where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0.

sections.label: Key Points:
points: Collection of rational numbers is denoted by Q (from "quotient").
All natural numbers, whole numbers, and integers are rational numbers.
Rational numbers do NOT have a unique p/q representation.
e.g., 1/2 = 2/4 = 10/20 = 25/50 = 47/94 — these are EQUIVALENT RATIONAL NUMBERS.
Standard (co-prime) form: p and q have no common factor other than 1.
e.g., 2/4 → co-prime form = 1/2.
There are INFINITELY MANY rational numbers between any two rational numbers.
To find a rational between r and s: use (r + s)/2 (the mean method).
To find n rational numbers between r and s:
write r = r(n+1)/n+1 and s = s(n+1)/n+1, then pick intermediate fractions.

EXAMPLE 1: True or False — Types of Numbers
Are the following statements true or false? Give reasons.
(i)   Every whole number is a natural number.
(ii)  Every integer is a rational number.
(iii) Every rational number is an integer.
Step 1: Check (i): Natural numbers = {1,2,3,...}, Whole numbers = {0,1,2,...}.
Zero is a whole number but NOT a natural number.
Step 2: Check (ii): Every integer m = m/1, which is of the form p/q (q=1≠0).
Step 3: Check (iii): 3/5 is rational but NOT an integer (integers have q=1).
(i) FALSE — 0 is a whole number but not a natural number.
(ii) TRUE — every integer m = m/1 is rational.
(iii) FALSE — 3/5 is rational but not an integer.

items.question: What is a rational number? State the set relationships N, W, Z, Q.
items.answer:
A number 'r' is RATIONAL if it can be written as p/q (p,q integers, q≠0). Symbol: Q.
Set relationships: N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q.
Every natural number, whole number, and integer is also rational.
(e.g., -3 = -3/1; 0 = 0/1; 5 = 5/1 — all rational.)

items.question: Is zero a rational number? Justify with three representations.
items.answer:
Yes. Zero can be written as p/q with q≠0 in multiple ways:
0 = 0/1 (p=0, q=1 ≠ 0) ✓
0 = 0/2 (p=0, q=2 ≠ 0) ✓
0 = 0/(-3) (p=0, q=-3 ≠ 0) ✓
Since zero satisfies the definition, 0 ∈ Q.
Zero belongs to W, Z, Q, and R.

items.question: What is the co-prime form of a rational number?
items.answer:
Co-prime form: p/q where HCF(p, q) = 1 (no common factor other than 1).
Express 15/35:
Step 1: HCF(15, 35) = 5. (15=3×5, 35=5×7)
Step 2: 15/35 = (15÷5)/(35÷5) = 3/7.
Check: HCF(3,7) = 1. ✓
Answer: 3/7 is the co-prime form of 15/35.

items.question: How many rational numbers exist between any two rational numbers?
items.answer:
There are INFINITELY MANY rational numbers between any two rational numbers.
Example: Between 1 and 2:
Mean method: (1+2)/2 = 3/2. → between 1 and 3/2: (1+3/2)/2 = 5/4.
We can always apply the mean method again to find another — endlessly.
So infinitely many rationals exist between any two.

items.question: Find six rational numbers between 3 and 4.
Are the following true or false? Give reasons:
items.answer:
(i) TRUE. N = {1,2,3,...} ⊂ W = {0,1,2,...}. Every element of N is in W.

(ii) FALSE. Z includes negatives: {...,-2,-1,0,1,2,...}. W = {0,1,2,...}.
Counter-example: -3 ∈ Z but -3 ∉ W.

(iii) FALSE. Rationals include fractions not in W.
Counter-example: 3/5 ∈ Q but 3/5 ∉ W.

items.question: Find five rational numbers between 1/4 and 1/2 using both
Using mean property find 4 rationals between 1/5 and 2/5.
items.answer:
Step 1: Mean of 1/5 and 2/5 = (1/5+2/5)/2 = (3/5)/2 = 3/10.
Step 2: Mean of 1/5 and 3/10 = (2/10+3/10)/2 = 5/20 = 1/4.
Step 3: Mean of 3/10 and 2/5 = (3/10+4/10)/2 = 7/20.
Step 4: Mean of 1/4 and 3/10 = (5/20+6/20)/2 = 11/40.
Answer: 1/4, 11/40, 3/10, 7/20.
Order: 1/5 < 1/4 < 11/40 < 3/10 < 7/20 < 2/5. ✓
Count: INFINITELY MANY rational numbers exist between any two rationals.

items.question: (i) Show 1/2 = 2/4 = 10/20 = 25/50. What are these called?
items.answer:
(i) Equivalent forms:
1/2 = (1×2)/(2×2) = 2/4 ✓
1/2 = (1×10)/(2×10) = 10/20 ✓
1/2 = (1×25)/(2×25) = 25/50 ✓
These are called EQUIVALENT RATIONAL NUMBERS (equivalent fractions).

(ii) Co-prime form:
1/2: HCF(1,2)=1 → co-prime form. ✓
2/4: HCF=2 → not co-prime.
10/20: HCF=10 → not co-prime.
25/50: HCF=25 → not co-prime.
Answer: 1/2 is the co-prime (standard) form.

(iii) -2005/2006:
p=-2005 (integer ✓), q=2006 (integer ✓), q≠0 ✓.
Yes, -2005/2006 is RATIONAL. It lies between -1 and 0 on number line.

---

PART A:

Denom = (5+1)×4 = 24.

Between 0.5 and 0.6 there are also: 0.501, 0.5001, 0.50001, ...
Also fractions: 51/100, 101/200, 201/400, ... — infinitely many.
Between ANY two rationals, INFINITELY MANY rationals exist.

PART B:

(iii) Three rational weights between 3/4 kg and 1 kg:
From (i): 19/24 ≈ 0.792 kg, 5/6 ≈ 0.833 kg, 7/8 = 0.875 kg.
Are they unique? NO — there are infinitely many choices.
Any rational between 3/4 and 1 is valid; we chose only 3 of infinitely many.

(iv) Relationship N ⊂ W ⊂ Z ⊂ Q ⊂ R:
- Every natural number is a whole number (0 is added in W).
- Every whole number is an integer (negatives added in Z).
- Every integer is rational (m = m/1, q=1≠0).
- Every rational is real (Q ⊂ R).
Example in ALL five: 5 ∈ N, 5 ∈ W, 5 ∈ Z, 5 ∈ Q, 5 ∈ R.
Example in Q only (not in Z): 3/5 ∈ Q but 3/5 ∉ Z, ∉ W, ∉ N.

sections.label: Definition:
sections.text:
A number 's' is called an IRRATIONAL NUMBER if it cannot be written in the form
p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0.

sections.label: Key Points:
points: First discovered by Pythagoreans (followers of Pythagoras) in Greece, ~400 BC.
The symbol sqrt( ) always refers to the POSITIVE square root.
e.g., sqrt(4) = 2 (not -2), though both 2 and -2 are square roots of 4.
Examples of irrationals: sqrt(2), sqrt(3), sqrt(5), sqrt(6), sqrt(7),
sqrt(10), sqrt(11), sqrt(12), sqrt(13), sqrt(14), sqrt(15), sqrt(17), pi,
0.10110111011110... (non-terminating non-recurring).
pi is irrational. 22/7 is only an approximation: pi ≠ 22/7.
REAL NUMBERS (R) = Rational numbers (Q) + Irrational numbers.
Every real number → unique point on the number line.
Every point on number line → unique real number.
Hence the number line is called the REAL NUMBER LINE.
Cantor (1845–1918) and Dedekind (1831–1916) proved this correspondence.

EXAMPLE 3: Locating sqrt(2) on the Number Line
PROBLEM: Locate sqrt(2) on the number line.
Step 1: Draw a unit square OABC with each side = 1 unit on paper.
Step 2: By Pythagoras theorem: OB = sqrt(OA^2 + AB^2) = sqrt(1^2 + 1^2) = sqrt(2).
Step 3: Transfer the figure to the number line with vertex O at zero (origin).
Step 4: Using a compass with centre O and radius OB = sqrt(2),
draw an arc intersecting the number line at point P.
ANSWER: The point P corresponds to sqrt(2) on the number line.
EXAMPLE 4: Locating sqrt(3) on the Number Line
PROBLEM: Locate sqrt(3) on the number line.
Step 1: Use the position of sqrt(2) already found (OB = sqrt(2) from Example 1.2.1).
Step 2: Construct BD perpendicular to OB with BD = 1 unit.
OD = sqrt(OB^2 + BD^2) = sqrt((sqrt(2))^2 + 1^2) = sqrt(2 + 1) = sqrt(3).
Step 4: Using compass with centre O and radius OD, draw arc intersecting
ANSWER: The point Q corresponds to sqrt(3) on the number line.
Note: In general, sqrt(n) can be located after sqrt(n-1) has been located,
by constructing a perpendicular of unit length.

sections.label: EXERCISE 1.2:
sections.raw:
1. State whether the following are true or false. Justify your answers.
(i)  Every irrational number is a real number.
[TRUE — R = Q + irrationals, so every irrational is real.]
(ii) Every point on the number line is of the form sqrt(m), where m is natural.
[FALSE — e.g., 2 is on the number line but not of the form sqrt(m) for
natural m. Also negative numbers are on it.]
(iii) Every real number is an irrational number.
[FALSE — rational numbers are also real, e.g., 1/2 is real but rational.]
2. Are the square roots of all positive integers irrational? If not, give an example
of a square root of a number that is a rational number.
[Ans: No. sqrt(4) = 2 (rational), sqrt(9) = 3 (rational).]
3. Show how sqrt(5) can be represented on the number line.
[Hint: sqrt(5) = sqrt((sqrt(4))^2 + 1^2) = sqrt(4+1). First locate sqrt(4)=2,
then construct perpendicular of 1 unit, giving OD = sqrt(5).]
4. Classroom Activity: Construct the 'square root spiral' showing sqrt(2), sqrt(3),
sqrt(4), ... using successive perpendiculars of unit length from the previous
hypotenuse.

items.question: Define irrational number. Who first discovered them?
items.answer:
IRRATIONAL: A number 's' that CANNOT be written as p/q (p,q integers, q≠0).
Discovery: PYTHAGOREANS in Greece (followers of Pythagoras) around 400 BC.
Hippacus of Croton proved sqrt(2) irrational. Theodorus showed sqrt(3), sqrt(5),
..., sqrt(17) also irrational.

items.question: What are real numbers? Write R = Q ∪ {irrationals}.
items.answer:
REAL NUMBERS (R) = All rational numbers + All irrational numbers.
R = Q ∪ {Irrational numbers}.
Key property: Every real number ↔ unique point on number line.
Every point on number line ↔ unique real number.
This correspondence is why the number line is called the REAL NUMBER LINE.

items.question: Is sqrt(4) irrational? Is sqrt(5) irrational? Give reasons.
items.answer:
sqrt(4): 4 = 2^2. sqrt(4) = 2 = 2/1 → RATIONAL. (Perfect square.)
sqrt(5): Not a perfect square. sqrt(5)=2.2360679...
Non-terminating non-recurring → IRRATIONAL.
Rule: sqrt(n) is irrational if n is a positive integer NOT a perfect square.

items.question: State approximate decimal values of sqrt(2) and pi.
items.answer:
sqrt(2) = 1.41421356237309504880...
pi = 3.14159265358979323846...
Is 22/7 = pi? NO.
22/7 = 3.142857bar (non-terminating RECURRING → rational).
pi = 3.14159265... (non-terminating NON-RECURRING → irrational).
22/7 ≠ pi. 22/7 is only an APPROXIMATION of pi.

items.question: Describe step-by-step how to locate sqrt(2) on the number line.
items.answer:
Step 1: Draw unit square OABC (each side = 1 unit) on paper.
Step 2: By Pythagoras: OB = sqrt(OA^2+AB^2) = sqrt(1+1) = sqrt(2).
Step 3: Transfer figure to number line with O at origin. OA along positive side.
Step 4: Compass radius OB = sqrt(2). Centre O. Draw arc cutting number line at P.
Result: P represents sqrt(2) on the number line. ✓

the "square root spiral."

items.question: Classify each as rational or irrational with justification:
items.answer:

(ii) sqrt(12) = sqrt(4×3) = 2sqrt(3) = 2×1.73205... = 3.46410...

(Non-zero rational × irrational = irrational.)

(iii) pi = 3.14159265... Non-terminating non-recurring.
Proved irrational by Lambert & Legendre (late 1700s). IRRATIONAL.
Note: 22/7 ≈ 3.14286 ≠ pi. It's only an approximation.

items.question: Locate sqrt(3) on the number line. Apply Pythagoras theorem
items.answer:
Stage 1 — Locate sqrt(2) first:
Step 1: Right triangle OAB: OA=AB=1. OB = sqrt(1+1) = sqrt(2).
Step 2: Arc from O, radius sqrt(2) → Point P1 = sqrt(2) on number line.

Stage 2 — Locate sqrt(3) using sqrt(2):
Step 3: At B, draw BD ⊥ OB with BD=1 unit.
Step 4: OD = sqrt(OB^2+BD^2) = sqrt((sqrt(2))^2+1) = sqrt(2+1) = sqrt(3).
Step 5: Arc from O, radius OD → Point P2 = sqrt(3) on number line. ✓
General: After locating sqrt(n-1), draw perpendicular of 1 unit → sqrt(n).

items.question: Classify the following with full justification:
items.answer:
(i) sqrt(23): 23 not a perfect square. sqrt(23)=4.7958... non-terminating non-recurring.
IRRATIONAL.

(ii) sqrt(225): 225=15^2. sqrt(225)=15=15/1. RATIONAL.

(iii) 0.3796: Terminating after 4 places. =3796/10000. RATIONAL.

(iv) 7.478478...: Block 478 repeats = 7.478bar. NON-TERMINATING RECURRING. RATIONAL.
(999x = 7471 → x = 7471/999.)

(v) 1.101001000100001...: Zeros between 1s: 1,2,3,4,... (increasing).
No fixed repeating block. NON-TERMINATING NON-RECURRING. IRRATIONAL.

items.question: Find an irrational number between 1/7 and 2/7. Justify.
items.answer:
Step 1: 1/7=0.142857bar, 2/7=0.285714bar.
Step 2: Construct non-terminating non-recurring decimal between them:
s = 0.1501500015000015...
(After each 1: zeros increase — 1,2,3,4,... No block repeats.)
Step 3: 0.142857... < 0.1501500... < 0.285714... ✓
Why irrational: Decimal is non-terminating non-recurring → IRRATIONAL.
Count: INFINITELY MANY irrational numbers exist between any two rationals.

5 ಮಾರ್ಕ್ಸ್ × 1 question:

PART A:

(i) NO. R = Q ∪ {irrationals}. Real numbers include BOTH types.
Rational reals: 1/2=0.5 (terminating), 1/3=0.3bar (recurring).
Irrational reals: sqrt(2)=1.41421... (non-recurring), pi=3.14159...
Not every real is irrational — all rationals are also real.

topics.topic_name: REAL NUMBERS AND THEIR DECIMAL EXPANSIONS

sections.label: Definition:
sections.text:
The DECIMAL EXPANSION of a real number is the representation of the number in
decimal (base-10) form. It reveals whether the number is rational or irrational.

sections.label: Key Points:
points: TERMINATING decimal: remainder becomes 0 after finite steps.
NON-TERMINATING RECURRING (repeating) decimal: remainder never 0, a block repeats.
(Bar notation: digits under bar repeat indefinitely.)
NON-TERMINATING NON-RECURRING: no block repeats — characteristic of irrationals.
Key theorem:
Rational → decimal expansion is terminating OR non-terminating recurring.
CONVERSE: terminating or non-terminating recurring → number is rational.
Irrational → decimal expansion is non-terminating non-recurring.
CONVERSE: non-terminating non-recurring → number is irrational.
For p/q rational, number of entries in repeating string < divisor q.
(e.g., for 1/7: divisor=7, repeating block has 6 digits: 142857)
Method to convert non-terminating recurring decimal to p/q:
Multiply by 10^(number of repeating digits) to shift and subtract.

items.question: Define terminating decimal. Give two examples.
items.answer:
TERMINATING decimal: the long division ends (remainder=0) after finite steps.
Examples:
1. 7/8 = 0.875 (ends in 3 steps). Terminating.
2. 1/2 = 0.5 (ends in 1 step). Terminating.
Key: Terminating decimals are always RATIONAL (= integer/10^n).

items.question: Define non-terminating recurring decimal. Give two examples with
items.answer:
NON-TERMINATING RECURRING: division never ends; a block of digits repeats.
Bar is placed over the repeating block.
Examples:
1. 10/3 = 3.3333... = 3.3bar (digit 3 repeats — 1-digit block).
2. 1/7 = 0.142857142857... = 0.142857bar (block 142857 — 6-digit block).
Key: Non-terminating recurring → always RATIONAL.

items.question: Convert 0.6bar to p/q form. Show steps.
What kind of decimal expansion does an irrational number have?
items.answer:
Irrational: NON-TERMINATING NON-RECURRING.
sqrt(2) = 1.41421356237309504880168...
Never terminates; computed to trillions of digits — no repeating block found.
Converse also true: non-terminating non-recurring → irrational.

Part 2 — 0.99999... = 1:

n/7 starts from where remainder n appears in cycle.

Check: 1/7 + 6/7 = 0.142857bar + 0.857142bar = 0.999999bar = 1. ✓

→ Non-terminating non-recurring → IRRATIONAL.

sections.label: Definition:
sections.text:
RATIONALISING THE DENOMINATOR means converting an expression with an irrational
denominator to an equivalent expression with a rational denominator, by
multiplying numerator and denominator by a suitable irrational expression.

sections.label: Key Points:
points: Rational numbers satisfy commutative, associative, distributive laws for + and ×.
Irrational numbers also satisfy these laws.
Closure properties:
(i)  Rational ± irrational = irrational (always).
(ii) Non-zero rational × irrational = irrational (always).
(iii) Irrational ± irrational = rational OR irrational.
e.g., sqrt(6)+(-sqrt(6))=0 (rational); sqrt(2)+sqrt(3) (irrational).
(iv) Irrational × irrational = rational OR irrational.
e.g., sqrt(2)×sqrt(2)=2 (rational); sqrt(2)×sqrt(3)=sqrt(6) (irrational).
Identities for positive real numbers a and b:
(i)   sqrt(ab) = sqrt(a) × sqrt(b)
(ii)  sqrt(a/b) = sqrt(a)/sqrt(b)
(iii) (sqrt(a)+sqrt(b))(sqrt(a)-sqrt(b)) = a - b
(iv)  (a+sqrt(b))(a-sqrt(b)) = a^2 - b
(v)   (sqrt(a)+sqrt(b))(sqrt(c)+sqrt(d)) = sqrt(ac)+sqrt(ad)+sqrt(bc)+sqrt(bd)
(vi)  (sqrt(a)+sqrt(b))^2 = a + 2sqrt(ab) + b
Conjugates used for rationalisation:
Conjugate of (sqrt(a)+sqrt(b)) is (sqrt(a)-sqrt(b)).
Conjugate of (a+sqrt(b)) is (a-sqrt(b)).
Geometric construction of sqrt(x) for any positive real x:
Mark AB=x, BC=1 on line. Find midpoint O of AC. Draw semicircle centre O,
radius OC. Draw perpendicular at B to meet semicircle at D. Then BD=sqrt(x).
nth roots: n-th root of a = a^(1/n) = b where b^n=a and b>0.
The symbol n√ is called the RADICAL SIGN.

sections.label: EXERCISE 1.4:
sections.raw:
1. Classify as rational or irrational:
(i)   2-sqrt(5): rational-irrational = irrational.
(ii)  (3+sqrt(23))-sqrt(23) = 3 = rational.
(iii) 2sqrt(7)/(7sqrt(7)) = 2/7 = rational.
(iv)  1/sqrt(2): irrational (non-zero rational/irrational = irrational).
(v)   2pi: irrational (non-zero rational × irrational = irrational).
2. Simplify:
(i)   (3+sqrt(3))(2+sqrt(2)) = 6+3sqrt(2)+2sqrt(3)+sqrt(6).
(ii)  (3+sqrt(3))(3-sqrt(3)) = 9-3 = 6.
(iii) (sqrt(5)+sqrt(2))^2 = 5+2sqrt(10)+2 = 7+2sqrt(10).
(iv)  (sqrt(5)-sqrt(2))(sqrt(5)+sqrt(2)) = 5-2 = 3.
3. pi=c/d (circumference/diameter). This seems like p/q, contradicting pi being
irrational. Resolution: c and d are not INTEGERS — they are real numbers.
The definition p/q requires p, q to be INTEGERS. Here c, d are real lengths.
4. Represent sqrt(9.3) on the number line:
Mark AB=9.3 units, BC=1 unit. Midpoint O of AC. Semicircle centre O, radius OC.
Perpendicular at B meets semicircle at D. Then BD = sqrt(9.3).
5. Rationalise denominators:
(i)   1/sqrt(7) = sqrt(7)/7.
(ii)  1/(sqrt(7)-sqrt(6)) = (sqrt(7)+sqrt(6))/(7-6) = sqrt(7)+sqrt(6).
(iii) 1/(sqrt(5)+sqrt(2)) = (sqrt(5)-sqrt(2))/(5-2) = (sqrt(5)-sqrt(2))/3.
(iv)  1/(sqrt(7)-2) = (sqrt(7)+2)/(7-4) = (sqrt(7)+2)/3.

items.question: State: (i) rational±irrational, (ii) non-zero rational×irrational.
items.answer:
(i) Rational ± irrational = IRRATIONAL (always).
Example: 2+sqrt(3) = 3.7320... non-recurring → irrational.

(ii) Non-zero rational × irrational = IRRATIONAL (always).
Example: 3×sqrt(2) = 4.2426... → irrational.

Note: 0×irrational = 0 (rational) — hence "non-zero" condition needed in (ii).

items.answer:

(iii) (sqrt(a)+sqrt(b))(sqrt(a)-sqrt(b)) = a-b

(v)   (sqrt(a)+sqrt(b))(sqrt(c)+sqrt(d)) = sqrt(ac)+sqrt(ad)+sqrt(bc)+sqrt(bd)

items.question: What is rationalising the denominator? Rationalise 1/sqrt(7).
items.answer:
RATIONALISING: converting an irrational denominator to a rational one by multiplying
numerator and denominator by a suitable irrational factor (rationalising factor).
Rationalise 1/sqrt(7):
1/sqrt(7) = (1×sqrt(7))/(sqrt(7)×sqrt(7)) = sqrt(7)/7.
Denominator is now 7 (rational). ✓

items.question: Find (sqrt(5)+sqrt(2))^2. State the identity used.
items.answer:
Identity: (sqrt(a)+sqrt(b))^2 = a+2sqrt(ab)+b. Here a=5, b=2.
= (sqrt(5))^2 + 2×sqrt(5)×sqrt(2) + (sqrt(2))^2
= 5 + 2sqrt(10) + 2 = 7+2sqrt(10).
Answer: (sqrt(5)+sqrt(2))^2 = 7+2sqrt(10).

Step 1: First: 5×2 = 10.
Step 2: Outer: 5×sqrt(5) = 5sqrt(5).
Step 3: Inner: sqrt(7)×2 = 2sqrt(7).
Step 4: Last: sqrt(7)×sqrt(5) = sqrt(35).
Combine: 10 + 5sqrt(5) + 2sqrt(7) + sqrt(35).
Answer: (5+sqrt(7))(2+sqrt(5)) = 10+5sqrt(5)+2sqrt(7)+sqrt(35).

Step 2: Multiply: 1/(2+sqrt(3)) × (2-sqrt(3))/(2-sqrt(3)).
Step 3: Denominator: identity (iv): (2+sqrt(3))(2-sqrt(3)) = 4-3 = 1.
Step 4: = (2-sqrt(3))/1 = 2-sqrt(3).
Answer: 1/(2+sqrt(3)) = 2-sqrt(3).
Check: (2-sqrt(3))×(2+sqrt(3)) = 4-3 = 1. ✓

items.answer:

Step 2: Multiply: 5/(sqrt(3)-sqrt(5)) × (sqrt(3)+sqrt(5))/(sqrt(3)+sqrt(5)).
Step 3: Denominator using identity (iii): (sqrt(3))^2-(sqrt(5))^2 = 3-5 = -2.
Step 4: = 5(sqrt(3)+sqrt(5))/(-2) = (-5/2)(sqrt(3)+sqrt(5)).
Answer: 5/(sqrt(3)-sqrt(5)) = (-5/2)(sqrt(3)+sqrt(5)).
Identity: (sqrt(a)+sqrt(b))(sqrt(a)-sqrt(b)) = a-b.

items.question: Describe geometric construction to find sqrt(3.5).
items.answer:
Construction:
Step 1: On a line, mark A. From A, mark B so AB=3.5. From B, mark C so BC=1.
AC = 3.5+1 = 4.5.
Step 2: Midpoint O of AC. OC = 4.5/2 = 2.25.
Step 3: Semicircle centre O, radius OC=2.25.
Step 4: At B, perpendicular to AC meets semicircle at D.
Step 5: Transfer BD to number line → represents sqrt(3.5).

Proof:
OD = 2.25 (radius). OB = OC-BC = 2.25-1 = 1.25.
BD^2 = OD^2-OB^2 = 2.25^2-1.25^2 = 5.0625-1.5625 = 3.5.
BD = sqrt(3.5). ✓

topics.topic_name: LAWS OF EXPONENTS FOR REAL NUMBERS

sections.label: Definition:
sections.text:
The LAWS OF EXPONENTS (laws of indices) are rules for simplifying expressions
involving powers. For a positive real number base with rational exponents,
these laws hold consistently.

sections.label: Key Points:
points: Laws for natural number exponents (a>0; m,n are natural numbers):
(i)   a^m × a^n = a^(m+n)       [Same base, multiply → add exponents]
(ii)  (a^m)^n = a^(mn)           [Power of power → multiply exponents]
(iii) a^m / a^n = a^(m-n), m>n   [Same base, divide → subtract exponents]
(iv)  a^m × b^m = (ab)^m         [Same exponent → multiply bases]
Also: a^0 = 1 (for a≠0); 1/a^n = a^(-n).
Fractional (rational) exponents:
a^(1/n) = n√a (nth root of a), where (a^(1/n))^n = a, a>0, n positive integer.
a^(m/n) = (n√a)^m = n√(a^m), where gcd(m,n)=1, n>0, a>0.
Also 4^(3/2) = (4^3)^(1/2) = 64^(1/2) = 8. [Both methods give same answer.]
The symbol n√ (nth root sign) is called the RADICAL SIGN.
Extended laws for rational exponents (a>0; p,q are rational numbers):
(i)   a^p × a^q = a^(p+q)
(ii)  (a^p)^q = a^(pq)
(iii) a^p / a^q = a^(p-q)
(iv)  a^p × b^p = (ab)^p

items.question: What is a^(1/n)? Give an example with n=3.
items.answer:
For a>0 and positive integer n: a^(1/n) = nth ROOT of a.

sections.text: A consolidated list of all key results studied in Chapter 1 on Number Systems.

sections.label: Key Points — Summary of Chapter 1:
points: 1. A number r is RATIONAL if it can be written as p/q (p,q integers, q≠0).
2. A number s is IRRATIONAL if it cannot be written as p/q (p,q integers, q≠0).
3. Decimal expansion of a rational number: TERMINATING or NON-TERMINATING RECURRING.
A number with terminating or non-terminating recurring decimal → RATIONAL.
4. Decimal expansion of an irrational: NON-TERMINATING NON-RECURRING.
A number with non-terminating non-recurring decimal → IRRATIONAL.
5. All rational + irrational numbers = REAL NUMBERS (R).
6. If r is rational and s is irrational (r≠0):
r+s and r-s are irrational; rs and r/s are irrational.
7. For positive real numbers a and b:
(i)   sqrt(ab) = sqrt(a)×sqrt(b)
(ii)  sqrt(a/b) = sqrt(a)/sqrt(b)
(iii) (sqrt(a)+sqrt(b))(sqrt(a)-sqrt(b)) = a-b
(iv)  (a+sqrt(b))(a-sqrt(b)) = a^2-b
(v)   (sqrt(a)+sqrt(b))^2 = a+2sqrt(ab)+b
8. To rationalise 1/(sqrt(a)+b), multiply by (sqrt(a)-b)/(sqrt(a)-b).
9. Extended laws of exponents (a>0; p,q rational):
(i)  a^p × a^q = a^(p+q)    (ii) (a^p)^q = a^(pq)
(iii) a^p / a^q = a^(p-q)   (iv) a^p×b^p = (ab)^p

items.question: Distinguish rational and irrational using decimal expansions.
items.answer:
RATIONAL: TERMINATING or NON-TERMINATING RECURRING decimal.
e.g., 7/8=0.875 (terminating); 1/3=0.3bar (non-terminating recurring).
IRRATIONAL: NON-TERMINATING NON-RECURRING decimal.
e.g., sqrt(2)=1.41421..., pi=3.14159...
Converse: Terminating/recurring → rational. Non-recurring → irrational.

items.question: Write the five identities for positive real numbers a and b
items.answer:
(i)   sqrt(ab) = sqrt(a)×sqrt(b)
(ii)  sqrt(a/b) = sqrt(a)/sqrt(b)
(iii) (sqrt(a)+sqrt(b))(sqrt(a)-sqrt(b)) = a-b
(iv)  (a+sqrt(b))(a-sqrt(b)) = a^2-b
(v)   (sqrt(a)+sqrt(b))^2 = a+2sqrt(ab)+b

items.question: If r is rational (r≠0) and s is irrational, state r+s, r-s, rs, r/s.
items.answer:
All four are IRRATIONAL when r≠0:
r+s = irrational.  r-s = irrational.
rs = irrational.   r/s = irrational.
Exception: r=0 → r×s=0 (rational). Hence r≠0 condition is essential.
Example: r=2, s=sqrt(3). 2+sqrt(3), 2-sqrt(3), 2sqrt(3), 2/sqrt(3) — all irrational.

items.question: Write the four extended laws of exponents (a>0, p,q rational).
items.answer:
(i)   a^p × a^q = a^(p+q)
(ii)  (a^p)^q = a^(pq)
(iii) a^p / a^q = a^(p-q)
(iv)  a^p × b^p = (ab)^p

items.question: Verify: (i) (sqrt(5)+sqrt(3))(sqrt(5)-sqrt(3))=2.
R = Q ∪ {irrationals}. Explain:
items.answer:
(i) sqrt(2) ∈ R: R includes all real numbers (rational+irrational). ✓
sqrt(2) ∉ Q: 1.41421... non-terminating non-recurring → cannot write as p/q.

(ii) 1/3 ∈ Q: 1/3 = p/q (p=1, q=3, q≠0). ✓
1/3 ∈ R: Since Q ⊂ R, every rational is also real. ✓

(iii) NO. Q and {irrationals} are DISJOINT: Q ∩ {irrationals} = ∅.
Every real number is EITHER rational OR irrational — never both.

items.question: Prove or disprove:
items.answer:
(i) 1.41421...+1.73205... = 3.14626... non-recurring. TRUE — IRRATIONAL. ✓

(ii) sqrt(2)×sqrt(8) = sqrt(16) = 4 = 4/1. TRUE — RATIONAL.
(Irrational×irrational CAN be rational.) ✓

(iii) pi=3.14159..., 22/7=3.14285... Difference = -0.00126... non-recurring.
Irrational - rational = irrational. TRUE — IRRATIONAL. ✓

(iv) 3/sqrt(3) = 3^(1-1/2) = 3^(1/2) = sqrt(3) = 1.73205...
sqrt(3) is IRRATIONAL, not rational.
FALSE. 3/sqrt(3) = sqrt(3) — IRRATIONAL. ✗

items.question: Rationalise 1/(sqrt(7)-sqrt(6)) and verify.
items.answer:
1/(sqrt(7)-sqrt(6)):
Conjugate = (sqrt(7)+sqrt(6)).
Denom = (sqrt(7))^2-(sqrt(6))^2 = 7-6 = 1.
= sqrt(7)+sqrt(6).
Verify: (sqrt(7)+sqrt(6))(sqrt(7)-sqrt(6)) = 7-6 = 1. ✓

1/(sqrt(7)-2):
Conjugate = (sqrt(7)+2).
Denom = (sqrt(7))^2-2^2 = 7-4 = 3.
= (sqrt(7)+2)/3.

items.answer:
Error in (sqrt(3)+sqrt(7))^2=10:
Student computed: (sqrt(3))^2+(sqrt(7))^2 = 3+7 = 10. WRONG.
Error: Missing middle term 2×sqrt(3)×sqrt(7) = 2sqrt(21).
Correct: 3+2sqrt(21)+7 = 10+2sqrt(21).
[2sqrt(21)≈9.165, so correct answer≈19.165, not 10.]

PART A:

(i) 0.47bar: x=0.4747...; 99x=47; x=47/99. RATIONAL. ✓
1.414213562... = sqrt(2) — non-terminating non-recurring → IRRATIONAL.
Both 47/99 ≈ 0.474 and sqrt(2) ≈ 1.414 are distinct points on the real number line.
R = Q ∪ {irrationals}; number line has ALL real numbers — no gaps.

(ii) 27^(2/3): 27^(1/3)=3 (3^3=27). 3^2=9. Answer: 9.
243^(3/5): 243^(1/5)=3 (3^5=243). 3^3=27. Answer: 27.

PART B:

(iii) Side = sqrt(50) = sqrt(25×2) = 5sqrt(2).
5sqrt(2)=5×1.41421...=7.07107... Non-recurring → IRRATIONAL.
On number line: Construct right triangle with legs 5 and 5.
Hypotenuse = sqrt(50) = 5sqrt(2). Transfer to number line.

(iv) Circumference = pi×1 = pi m.
pi = 3.14159265... Non-terminating non-recurring → IRRATIONAL.
22/7≈3.14286 ≠ pi (22/7 only an approximation).
Circumference = pi m — IRRATIONAL.
Note: pi = c/d but c and d are real lengths (not integers) — the rational
definition p/q requires INTEGER numerator and denominator.
